content: Food intolerance, also referred to as food sensitivity, is a negative reaction to certain foods that may or may not involve the immune system or food poisoning. It can result from the absence of specific enzymes or chemicals required for digestion or from the body’s reaction to certain natural or artificial food components. Symptoms of food intolerance can vary widely and are often mistaken for food allergies. Unlike true allergies, which involve a rapid IgE-mediated immune response, food intolerance may involve a delayed IgG-mediated response, making it challenging to identify the offending food. This delayed response separates the cause and symptoms over time, complicating diagnosis. A deficiency in digestive enzymes is a common cause of food intolerance. For example, lactose intolerance occurs when the body produces insufficient lactase to break down lactose in milk. Gluten intolerance, on the other hand, damages the villi in the small intestine, impairing the absorption of water and nutrients. Another type of intolerance involves sensitivity to food chemicals, such as salicylates, which are naturally present in many foods. Salicylate sensitivity can cause symptoms like hives, stomach pain, headaches, mouth ulcers, and has even been linked to conditions like ADD and ADHD. Food intolerance can exist as an isolated condition or contribute to complex syndromes such as Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME), Post-Viral Fatigue Syndrome (PVFS), or conditions like Leaky Gut Syndrome. Due to the complexity of these conditions, diagnosis is best performed by experienced practitioners. Symptoms of food intolerance include gastrointestinal issues like gas, diarrhea, constipation, and irritable bowel syndrome, as well as skin rashes, migraines, and respiratory symptoms like an unproductive cough. Reactions to dietary chemical components are more common than true food allergies. These reactions can be triggered by natural organic chemicals found in plants and other foods, as well as by artificial additives, preservatives, colorings, and flavorings. Both natural and artificial ingredients can provoke adverse reactions in sensitive individuals, with the degree of sensitivity varying between people. Reactions to natural food chemicals are often more insidious and harder to diagnose. Chemical intolerance can occur in individuals from both allergic and non-allergic family backgrounds, and symptoms can manifest at any age, either suddenly or gradually. Triggers may include dietary changes, viral infections, or serious illnesses, particularly those associated with sudden weight loss. Environmental chemical exposure and drug reactions can also play a role. Women are more commonly affected by chemical intolerance, possibly due to hormonal differences, as many food chemicals mimic hormones. Symptoms can affect the skin, respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract (GIT), and central nervous system (CNS), either individually or in combination. Common symptoms include urticaria, angioedema, migraines, and irritable bowel syndrome. Respiratory symptoms may include nasal congestion, sinusitis, pharyngeal irritation, and asthma. GIT symptoms include mouth ulcers, abdominal cramps, nausea, bloating, diarrhea, constipation, and irregular bowel movements. CNS symptoms can be diverse, leading to misdiagnoses of neurosis or hysteria. These symptoms may include headaches, lethargy, myalgia, memory loss, concentration difficulties, mental agitation, depression, dysphasia, visual disturbances, dizziness, tinnitus, autonomic disturbances, paresthesias, and neuralgias. Fatigue, sudden energy loss, or chronic lack of energy are also frequently reported. The most widely distributed natural food chemical capable of provoking reactions is salicylate, found in foods like apples, citrus fruits, strawberries, tomatoes, and wine. Cross-reactions with tartrazine and benzoic acid are well-documented. However, significant amounts of benzoates and salicylates naturally occur in many foods, including fruits, juices, vegetables, spices, herbs, nuts, tea, wine, and coffee. Other common reactive chemicals include amines, monosodium glutamate (MSG), nitrates, and certain antioxidants. Chemicals involved in aroma and flavor are often implicated. It is important to note that classifying or avoiding foods based on botanical families is irrelevant to their chemical content and is not useful in managing food intolerance. Excluding single foods does not necessarily identify the responsible chemical, as multiple chemicals may be present in a single food. Many individuals are sensitive to several food chemicals, and reactions are more likely when foods are consumed in combinations that exceed sensitivity thresholds. Some individuals may react to even trace amounts of certain chemicals. Food intolerance can also lead to fluid retention, as offending foods may increase capillary permeability, causing extra water to enter cells and result in swelling. Bloating may also indicate fluid retention or improper gastrointestinal handling of certain foods, both of which can contribute to excess weight. Research suggests a link between food intolerance, poor digestion, and a slower metabolism. Diagnosis of food intolerance often involves elimination and challenge testing. Clinical investigations are typically reserved for severe cases, as minor complaints that do not significantly impact lifestyle may not warrant the inconvenience of extensive testing. Treatment generally involves avoiding the offending foods and gradually re-establishing tolerance. Minor dietary changes to exclude foods causing obvious reactions may suffice for many individuals without professional assistance. However, for those unable to identify problem foods or experiencing severe symptoms, expert medical and dietary guidance is recommended. Dietetic departments in teaching hospitals are a good starting point for such assistance. Elimination diets are designed to exclude food chemicals likely to cause reactions, as well as foods commonly associated with true allergies or enzyme deficiencies. These diets are not intended for everyday use but rather to isolate problematic foods and chemicals. Avoiding foods with additives is also essential during this process. During elimination, individuals may experience withdrawal symptoms, masking effects, or further sensitization. Foods considered must-haves may indicate potential food addictions, including tea, coffee, chocolate, and health foods, as they all contain food chemicals. The elimination process helps unmask problem foods, allowing patients to associate cause and effect. It typically takes about five days of total abstinence to unmask a food or chemical, with withdrawal symptoms often occurring during the first week. Residual traces may take at least two weeks to clear. If symptoms persist after six weeks, food intolerance is unlikely, and a normal diet should be resumed. Challenge testing can begin after at least two weeks of symptom reduction or five days of no symptoms. This involves reintroducing selected foods containing only one food chemical to isolate reactions. In some countries, purified food chemicals in capsule form are available for testing, often combined with placebo capsules for control purposes. This method provides more definitive results. New challenges should only be introduced after 48 hours if no reactions occur or after five days of no symptoms following a reaction. Over time, individuals avoiding food chemicals may build resistance through controlled exposure to small amounts, aiming to establish a varied and nutritionally adequate diet. IgG blood tests detect antibody reactions in the blood, requiring only a small sample, sometimes obtained via a pinprick. The presence of food-specific IgG antibodies indicates a reaction to a particular food, with the level of IgG correlating to the degree of intolerance. Once problematic food chemicals are identified, a dietitian or healthcare professional can prescribe an appropriate diet to avoid these foods. Lists of suitable foods are available from hospitals and patient support groups, which can also provide advice on local food brands. A dietitian ensures adequate nutrition with safe foods and supplements if necessary. Cross-reactivity is a common phenomenon in food intolerance, where individuals intolerant to certain foods may develop intolerance to others with similar molecular or protein structures. For example, someone reacting to peanuts may also react to chickpeas or lentils, as they belong to the same legume family. This means that symptoms may persist even when avoiding the initially identified problematic foods.
